How to read the map

The legend explains what each layer means. Hover cards give fast contextual facts, while the right-side panels open deeper profiles with indicators, ports and route logic.

Good workflow: hover → open profile → save the strongest examples → reuse them in case studies.

Why this matters

The Atlas separates official economic observations, logistics geography and contextual route models.

Coverage and limitations

Source coverage differs by subject and year. Port throughput, connectivity and inland logistics are shown only where records or geographic context are available.

Case studies

Geography, logistics and evidence

Research examples connect geographic and economic context with logistics stages, cited observations and explicit limitations.

Illustrative logistics scenario

Japan → East Asia → Russian Far East: illustrative machinery scenario

This educational logistics model separates inspection, export preparation, transfer and destination distribution. The displayed geography is illustrative: it does not establish a current commercial service, product eligibility or a legally compliant itinerary. It is not a legal determination, a customs instruction or a confirmed itinerary. An intermediate country does not change product origin or legal obligations. Operational availability requires separate verification.

Inspection and identificationDocument the machine model, serial number and condition so the same asset can be identified across handovers.
Export gatewayYokohama and Nagoya provide geographic examples for discussing export preparation and terminal handling. Packaging and transfer stages are concepts, not confirmation of a service.
East Asian connectionAn East Asian gateway is shown as an illustrative transfer or consolidation concept. It establishes neither an actual itinerary nor a change in product origin or legal eligibility.
Far East gateway and distributionVladivostok is a geographic example for separating port handling, inland transfer and destination distribution. The model does not verify operational access or a commercial service.
Atlas research context

Why Poland matters as a Baltic logistics gateway

Gdańsk and Gdynia connect maritime access with Central European production and consumption. Port performance therefore depends on inland links as well as quay capacity. A defensible comparison separates container activity from energy and bulk cargo, and compares the same year and port boundary.

Atlas research context

South Korea and Hong Kong: different network roles

South Korea illustrates manufacturing-linked exports, while Hong Kong highlights re-export and intermediation. Comparing gross export totals without distinguishing origin, re-export and value added can overstate similarities. The Atlas sector labels are context; precise shares require matched official product records.

Atlas research context

Russia’s Pacific, Baltic and Black Sea windows

Vladivostok and Vostochny face Pacific networks; St. Petersburg connects to the Baltic; Novorossiysk provides Black Sea access. These are different geographic systems, not interchangeable terminals. Inland distance, cargo specialization and changing access conditions matter when interpreting trade geography.

Atlas research context

Mombasa: the hinterland is part of the port story

Mombasa’s gateway role extends beyond Kenya’s coastline through inland East African corridors. Port handling, border coordination and inland connections form a linked system. A rise in gateway cargo should not automatically be interpreted as growth in Kenyan production.

Atlas research context

Santos links farming and industry with ocean trade

Santos illustrates how a port can serve containerized industrial goods and agricultural bulk flows. The same port name can conceal different terminal and transport systems. Product choice changes the relevant cargo metric, inland chain and seasonality; one TEU statistic cannot describe the whole gateway.

Atlas research context

Tanger Med: manufacturing meets a maritime passage

Tanger Med combines gateway and transshipment functions near the Strait of Gibraltar. Automotive production adds a manufacturing connection to the geographic advantage. Gateway exports and transshipment should be separated when assessing how port activity relates to the national economy.

How to use saved research

Sources & methodology

What is live, what is curated

The site deliberately separates official statistics from editorial route and logistics explanations.

World Bank World Development Indicators

Country profiles, comparison tables, rankings and time-series charts request merchandise exports, merchandise imports and GDP through the World Bank API.

Indicators API documentation ↗
UN Comtrade

The Products tab can request official merchandise trade by commodity. The module is loaded on demand because data availability, API limits and reporting years can vary.

UN Comtrade ↗
UNCTAD Data Hub

Maritime connectivity, port connectivity, container throughput and seaborne-trade datasets are the recommended next layer for deeper port research.

UNCTADstat Data Centre ↗
Atlas editorial layer

Country roles, port lists, product tags, chokepoint explanations and route models are curated educational context. Important claims should be checked against current official port, customs and trade-agency sources.

About the Atlas

A research tool, not just a globe

Global Trade Atlas connects economic indicators with ports, products, strategic maritime passages and representative supply-chain corridors.

Country intelligence

Enhanced profiles for selected economies: indicators, sectors, partners and logistics gateways within global geographic coverage.

Logistics geography

Ports and chokepoints turn the map from political geography into a transport-network view.

Research transparency

Official numerical sources are kept separate from manually curated explanations and route models.
